title: Voice AI Turns a Throttled CPU Into a Duplicate Reply
dek: Most voice agent bugs are not in the model. They hide in turn detection timers, CPU quotas, native threads and serial tool calls. Here is where to look first.
by: Draft for team review · written by Claude Code from published research and engineering writing · checked in code
lead: How do AI voice agents work? As a relay of turn detection, speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech. Most failures live in that relay's CPU timing and threads, so isolate calls and watch throttling.

cover.alt: One sentence delivered with a gap of late chunks; the silence timer splits it into two LLM turns and two replies.
cover.caption: Late audio from a throttled pod looks exactly like a pause, so one sentence becomes two turns.

description: How do AI voice agents work, and why do they reply twice? A field guide to turn detection, throttled CPUs, leaked threads and faster tool calls.

body.text: Give turn detection a CPU it never waits for

body: A caller says one sentence and hears two replies. That is the classic voice AI failure, and one engineering team traced it to a starved process [1]. Their agent runs a fixed relay [1]. Voice activity detection (VAD) spots speech, speech-to-text (STT) transcribes it, an LLM answers, and text-to-speech (TTS) speaks the answer back [1].

That relay is how AI voice agents work, and VAD decides when a turn ends. In this stack it is Silero, an ONNX model scoring short audio chunks, plus a silence timer called `stop_secs` [1]. Once the speech score stays under a threshold for that long, the transcript goes to the LLM [1]. Here is the catch. The timer runs on wall-clock time [1].

Under a tight CPU limit, audio chunks arrive late, and late chunks look like silence [1]. The kernel bills CPU in 100 ms slices against the quota, so short spikes get throttled even when the average looks idle [1]. VAD then ends the turn mid-sentence. The rest arrives as a second turn, and the caller gets two answers [1].

The team first patched it with a longer STT timeout, then spent months loosening VAD thresholds [1]. Some of that tuning, the author admits, was compensating for a starved process [1]. We think this is the lesson worth stealing. Before you tune a turn detector, prove it gets its CPU on time.

body.text: Watch throttled periods instead of average CPU

body: The author's first suspect was Python's global interpreter lock, the GIL, which lets only one thread run Python code at a time [1]. Measurements cleared it. Resampling and VAD inference run in C and C++ underneath, release the GIL and use two cores happily [1]. The real limit was the pod's CPU budget. Extra threads simply spend that budget faster [1].

Each call held a WebRTC peer, two vendor WebSockets and one SSE stream [1]. It also ran an ONNX model that scored the audio roughly 30 times each second [1]. Most CPU went into speech traffic: chunking and sending audio to STT, parsing transcripts, cutting TTS audio into 20 ms frames and encoding Opus [1]. No single stage is heavy. Each one is a spike.

So average CPU lies here. The author recommends tracking throttled periods as a share of all CPU periods, because dashboards flatten spikes into a calm line [1]. Their load tester simulates whole calls, with real STT and mocked TTS and LLM that keep measured vendor latencies [1]. An instant mock, they warn, inflates a pod's apparent capacity several times over [1].

body.label: Illustrative check: read the throttled share from a container's cgroup
body.source:
def throttled_share(path="/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat"):
    stats = dict(line.split() for line in open(path))
    periods = int(stats["nr_periods"])
    throttled = int(stats["nr_throttled"])
    if not periods:
        return None          # no data yet: unknown, never zero
    return throttled / periods

# page on a rising throttled share, not on average CPU use

body.text: Count threads when memory only climbs

body: Memory told a stranger story. Over two days, three pods climbed in a staircase that never stepped down [1]. Python asyncio code does not spawn OS threads by the score, so something native did [1]. The Daily WebRTC client, wrapped by a Python library, starts roughly ten OS threads for each call. Only its `release()` method frees them [1].

body.alt: Schematic: pod memory rising one step per ended call until the memory limit, while a gauge reads zero.
body.caption: Each call that ended without releasing its native client left a step that never came back down.

body: Under load, teardown timed out and fell back to cancelling the Python task [1]. Cancelling the coroutine never called `release()`. The Python object was collected, but the native threads and audio buffers stayed [1]. Worse, the gauge of active transports dropped to zero once the reference went away [1]. The metric said clean. The kernel saw a growing pile of OS threads.

The fixes that failed are instructive. A bigger memory limit only slowed the crash, and a Python heap profiler saw nothing because the leak was native [1]. Forced garbage collection and a different allocator could not free what nothing had released [1]. The real fix was small. Shield the release call from cancellation, and drop the transport entry only after it finishes [1].

body.text: Give each call its own process

body: The team's comparison pinned all three problems on one variable: how many calls a pod carried [1]. VAD jitter grew faster than linearly with calls per pod, and STT and TTS load grew linearly [1]. The native leak grew with every call the pod had ever served [1]. So the design changed. A pod would serve one call and then exit, like a game server [1].

With one call per process, nothing can leak between calls, and VAD never competes with a neighbour's TTS [1]. Routing becomes trivial, because each call uses the pod it was handed [1]. Even the earlier consistent-hashing work only mattered because each pod kept state for several calls at once [1]. The hard part moves to scheduling fresh processes fast enough, which the follow-up post builds on Agones and Karpenter [1].

body.text: Then nothing leaks across calls, because there is no across calls.

body: We agree with the move, and with the candour of the write-up. Multi-tenant realtime Python is hard to keep fair. Per-call isolation turns three bugs into one capacity question. The price is a warm pool of ready processes to manage, so measure startup time before you copy the design.

body.text: Speculate on tool calls while the user is still talking

body: Tool calls add a second wait. A typical speech assistant runs recognition, then the LLM, then any external tool, one after another [2]. So the tool's delay starts only after the user stops and the LLM has chosen a call [2]. A new arXiv paper on on-device voice agents starts the tool earlier [2].

body.alt: Bars: median time-to-first-audio 5.79 s serial against 4.60 s speculative; spread 3.49 s against 2.81 s.
body.caption: Starting tools during speech cut both the typical wait and its spread.

body.text: As a final safeguard, the LLM retains the ability to issue tool calls directly, ensuring that the latency of our framework is upper-bounded by the baseline serial execution pipeline in the worst case.

body: A Predictor module reads partial ASR hypotheses, the running guesses a recogniser makes mid-utterance [2]. It anticipates tool calls, runs them speculatively and caches the results [2]. When the turn ends, valid cached outputs go into the LLM prompt [2]. A rule-based check drops results that a self-correction made stale, and the LLM can still call tools itself [2].

On a fully built Android assistant, live measurements showed median time-to-first-audio falling from 5.79 s to 4.60 s [2]. The standard deviation shrank from 3.49 s to 2.81 s, so waits became more predictable [2]. We value the worst-case bound more than the median gain. A speed layer that cannot make things slower is easy to ship.

Acting on partial speech has a gentler use, too. A paper on Bangla speech pairs a transformer transcriber with a BiLSTM attention model that completes sentences people with dementia leave unfinished [3]. In both cases, a model guesses the rest of an utterance. Both need a clean way to back out when the guess is wrong.

body.text: Weigh transcription errors by their consequence

body: Word error rate counts mistakes. It never asks what they break. A new arXiv paper on ASR metrics points out that errors of similar size can do very different damage to the situation the speech describes [4]. Judging that needs an understanding of what the speech sets up or tries to achieve [4].

LLM judges can make that call, but they add cost and scoring variability [4]. The SITAR metric moves the judgment offline. Its framework rolls situational severity and cumulative extent into one bounded score [4]. Using limited offline LLM help to build training targets, the authors train a small BERT-family regressor [4]. It scores a reference and hypothesis pair in one forward pass [4].

The authors report that SITAR tracks broad capability scaling and adds diagnostic signal that sits apart from existing metrics [4]. They pitch it as a complement to current ASR metrics, and we agree with that framing [4]. For a voice agent, add your own critical phrases too. Amounts, names and negations are where one wrong word costs most.

body.text: Version your watermark detector like an API

body: The speaking side has its own risks. The Gemini 3.8 text-to-speech release, discussed on Hacker News, offered voice replication from a 30-second sample [5]. The announcement paired it with consent verification, SynthID watermarking and C2PA credentials [5]. Commenters argued that local tools already clone voices well and that a local pass could strip such marks [5]. One described fine-tuning Qwen3-TTS 1.7B on about 12 minutes of recordings using an RTX 3090 [5].

Detection has a quieter failure. A new arXiv paper on zero-bit audio watermarking, which only answers marked or unmarked, studies what happens when versions change [6]. Real deployments update embedders and detectors and split them apart [6]. A new detector can then miss content marked by older embedders. It can also raise false positives on embedders it was never meant to recognise [6].

The authors train each new detector against a chain of frozen legacy embedders, sampled by performance [6]. That coupling causes embedder collapse, which badly hurts the true negative rate against embedders outside the chain [6]. An Angular Diversity Loss pushes each new embedder into its own region of the output space [6]. Together, they restore near-perfect true negative rates without hurting detection or audio quality [6]. We read this as API versioning. Test every detector against every embedder you shipped.

body.text: Keep voice out of jobs people need to scan

body: Voice is slow to skim. Even with speculation, the Android assistant's median wait before the first audio was 4.60 s [2]. Listeners on Hacker News also complained that leading voices exaggerate emotion and wander from the prompt [5]. Some just wanted a plain, restrained computer voice [5]. For tables, codes, prices and anything a user must compare or copy, text on a screen wins.

Skip voice, too, when you cannot establish consent for a voice you plan to clone [5]. And skip it when nobody on your team can own a realtime process, because the failures above lived in CPU quotas and native threads [1]. A chat box is not glamorous. It rarely gives anyone two answers to one sentence.
How do AI voice agents work?

Most run a relay of components. Voice activity detection decides when you stopped talking, speech-to-text transcribes the turn, an LLM writes a reply, and text-to-speech speaks it [1]. Tools usually run after the LLM picks them, which adds delay [2]. Each hop adds latency, and the turn detector's silence timer is often the most fragile part [1].
Why does my voice AI agent answer twice?

Often because the turn detector saw a gap that was really late audio. One team found that CPU throttling delayed audio chunks, so the silence timer ended the turn mid-sentence [1]. The second half then arrived as a new turn and got its own reply [1]. Watch CPU throttling before you retune the detector.
How can I reduce voice agent latency?

Start slow work before the user finishes speaking. One on-device assistant predicted tool calls from partial transcripts and ran them early [2]. Its median time to first audio fell from 5.79 s to 4.60 s, and the LLM could still call tools itself as a fallback [2]. Keeping each call in its own process also stops neighbours stealing CPU [1].
